title: Timothy Shanahan Points to a Possible Speech-to-Print Advantage
author: Harriett Janetos
summary: Janetos responds to Timothy Shanahan's discussion of speech-to-print versus print-to-speech approaches to beginning reading. She clarifies that Linguistic Phonics, following Diane McGuinness, unites phonemic awareness with letters from the start rather than teaching sounds before print. Her case is that encoding comes first and feeds decoding, because spelling is harder than reading and forces fuller orthographic representations. She traces the historical research Shanahan cites, lists the elements of the McGuinness prototype alongside researchers whose work aligns with each, and agrees with Shanahan that the evidence is indirect but substantial. The post argues that efficiency matters in classrooms with limited time, and calls for humility and less tribalism in choosing reading methods. It leans heavily on quotation but her framing and argument are clear.
points: Speech-to-print approaches teach children to identify and sequence sounds with letters, integrating writing and spelling into every reading lesson.
Spelling demands fuller orthographic detail than reading, which may explain the brain boost from practising encoding alongside decoding.
Shanahan judges the evidence supportive but indirect; Janetos argues that efficiency under classroom time pressure strengthens the case even if effectiveness is merely equal.
Practical components include early phonemic awareness with letters, invented spelling, explicit spelling instruction and building words from sounds.
She urges selecting methods on evidence and fit rather than tribal loyalty or tradition.
quotes: This union of phonemic awareness (PA) with phonics means our students are simultaneously focusing their attention on their language sounds and the letters and spellings representing those sounds. Discussing their 2024 meta-analysis, Florina Erbeli and Marianne Rice emphasize that both PA with and without letters improved phonemic awareness—but it was PA with letters that improved reading and spelling.

This distinction between auditory and visual signals may explain Timothy Shanahan’s stated disconnect between learning to read and reading, which seems counterintuitive until we consider that humans as a species began—and humans as individuals begin—speaking long before they began and begin reading. Therefore, reading instruction that recruits what the brain has been primed for might create the optimal conditions that promote efficient recognition of how letters represent speech.

Encoding is the entry point to learning how to decode. While we know that traditional phonics programs do include writing, in S2P writing is an integral part of reading to the extent that dictation often precedes practice with reading decodable text, and this approach teaches students to say the phonemes as they write the graphemes. Spelling is a noisy affair.

Speech-to-Print advocates like me have been satisfied for a long time despite lack of definitive proof because we see how much more efficient this approach is, even if it is only equally effective as the best P2S approaches.

Steve Dykstra cautions that a lack of bullseye evidence for a particular instructional method shouldn’t automatically rule out that method if it can be part of making reasonable decisions that we believe will benefit our students. He says: We are not required to be right; we are required to have ‘right’ reasons that we can explain to other professionals . . . Know where the science ends and your best judgment begins.

Finally—and most important—let’s cultivate curiosity and show humility as we examine the best reading instruction methods available. Let’s be highly selective and choose methods that align with best practices regardless of their origin, freeing decision-making from trends and traditions that may not be serving our students in the best possible ways.
There is too much tribalism and not enough trial and error in considering new and/or repurposed approaches to reading instruction. Let’s make changes that really make a difference. That’s the point.
